source: v² = v₀² + 2aΔx links speeds and displacement when the time isn't known.
Students forget the 2, or take a square root and lose the velocity's direction.

Sometimes the time is neither given nor wanted: a car's braking distance, a jet's runway length. You could find $t$ first from the constant-acceleration equations, but one more equation skips that step.

$\role{velocity}{v}^2 = \role[initial velocity]{velocity}{v_0}^2 + 2\role{acceleration}{a}\role[displacement]{position}{\Delta x}$ links the speeds and the displacement without the time. It also needs constant acceleration.

Start from the area under the straight $v$–$t$ line: a trapezoid, $\Delta x = \tfrac12(v_0 + v)\,t$. The first equation gives $t = \dfrac{v - v_0}{a}$. Substitute: $$\Delta x = \dfrac{(v + v_0)(v - v_0)}{2a} = \dfrac{v^2 - v_0^2}{2a}.$$ Multiply both sides by $2a$ and the time is gone: $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$.
A car braking from 20 m/s at 5 m/s²: the triangle under the v–t line is the 40 m stopping distance.
A car moving at $25\ \text{m/s}$ brakes at $5\ \text{m/s}^2$. How far does it go while stopping?
A skier at $4\ \text{m/s}$ speeds up at $2\ \text{m/s}^2$ over $30\ \text{m}$ of slope. Find the final speed.
A jet must reach $70\ \text{m/s}$ from rest on a $1{,}400\ \text{m}$ runway. What acceleration does it need?
The four constant-acceleration equations. Pick the one that leaves out the quantity you neither know nor want.
Because $\Delta x = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2|a|}$ when stopping, doubling the speed makes the braking distance four times as long, not twice. Traffic engineers build that square into stopping-distance tables.

Forgetting the 2 in $2a\Delta x$, or stopping at $v^2$ and forgetting the square root. Also, the square root only gives a size: $v^2 = 36$ means $v = +6$ or $-6\ \text{m/s}$, and you choose the sign from the direction of motion. Check: units of $2a\Delta x$ are $\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$, the same as $v^2$.
